one_liner: Literal-only, grep-style recursive search tool in C with ARM64 NEON assembly kernels; claims 6.7x over ripgrep on the author's private tree.
what_it_does: A command-line searcher (`chingrep`, alias `cg`) for fixed strings across a directory tree or stdin, with grep-like flags: -i (ASCII only), -w, -c, -l, -m, --include/--exclude globs, --exclude-dir, --no-ignore and --files. It is not a drop-in for ripgrep or grep: there is no regex engine (every pattern is a literal), no -v, no context lines (-A/-B/-C), unknown flags are silently ignored, and output lines from different files interleave because all worker threads share one mutex-guarded 64 KiB buffer.
how_it_is_fast: The case-sensitive ARM64 kernel (src/asm/simd_arm64.s) compares the needle's first and last bytes against 16-byte NEON windows and AND-s the masks, verifying candidates byte by byte; memchr, the 512-byte NUL probe and the newline counter are 64-byte unrolled NEON. On x86_64 the same first/last-byte filter is AVX2 intrinsics in C (Mula's generic SIMD substring idea). Files are mmap-ed with MADV_SEQUENTIAL/MADV_WILLNEED, the walker uses readdir d_type instead of lstat, and the pool sizes itself to Apple P-cores via sysctl hw.perflevel0.physicalcpu. Most of the measured gap, however, plausibly comes from searching fewer files: the walker always skips any file or directory named .git, node_modules, dist, build, target, coverage, .next, .nuxt, .idea, .vscode or .DS_Store.
when_to_use: Reading or borrowing a small, MIT-licensed example of a NEON first/last-byte substring filter, NEON memchr and a NEON newline counter on Apple Silicon.
Personal ad-hoc literal searches on macOS/Apple Silicon over JavaScript/web project trees where skipping node_modules, dist and build is what you want anyway.
Benchmarking experiments where you deliberately control both tools' file sets (for example cg --no-ignore against rg -uu, or both given the same explicit file list).
when_not_to_use: Any search that needs regular expressions, inverted matches, context lines, Unicode case folding or exact .gitignore semantics; ripgrep provides all of these.

Trees with source directories or files named build, dist, target or coverage (Chromium's top-level build/, many CMake and Bazel layouts): cg silently skips them unless --no-ignore, which also disables .gitignore handling.

Linux: src/core/pool.c includes <sys/sysctl.h> and calls sysctlbyname unconditionally (the header was removed in glibc 2.32 and sysctlbyname is BSD/macOS-only), and the ARM64 .s files export Mach-O underscore symbols, so the README's Linux support looks unbuilt and untested.
Case-insensitive searches on ARM64: arm64_search_literal_icase is a plain scalar byte-at-a-time O(n*m) loop with no NEON at all.
x86_64 machines without AVX2: the Makefile builds the x86 target with -mavx2 -mfma and the 'dispatcher' is compile-time only, so the binary has no runtime fallback.

integration.form: static binary built with make (CLI tool; no library API)
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and pthreads (macOS sysctlbyname required by pool.c)
integration.min_toolchain: clang or gcc with GNU assembler syntax for AArch64; Makefile defaults to clang -O3; no version stated
integration.platforms: macOS on Apple Silicon (tested by the author); x86_64 requires AVX2 at build and run time; Linux builds likely fail (sys/sysctl.h, sysctlbyname, Mach-O symbol names)
integration.thread_safety: Process-level tool; one shared output buffer behind a mutex, workers pull paths from a mutex/condvar queue of 65,536 slots
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — accepts a grep-like subset of flags for literal patterns, but needs -r where rg recurses by default, has no regex, and applies different ignore rules (hard-coded name skips, no hidden-file skipping, no negation rules)

gotchas: Line-number bug found in this enrichment: src/asm/newline_count.s accumulates up to 64 iterations x 4 vectors = 256 hits per 8-bit lane, one more than a byte holds, so a lane wraps to 0 whenever all 256 of its positions in a 4 KiB block are newlines. Emulating the kernel, a file of 1,000 lines of 16 bytes counts 232 newlines and 5,000 blank lines count 904, so -n (on by default) prints wrong line numbers for runs of blank lines or fixed-width lines whose length divides 16. The comment says the block size was chosen to prevent exactly this overflow; 63 iterations would.

Unequal work in the arena: cg skips the hard-coded directory names above plus anything matched by any .gitignore (even outside a git repository) and ignores '!' negation rules, while rg skips hidden files that cg searches and honours .gitignore only inside git repositories. Scenario 16 also compares cg --exclude-dir=test, which prunes every directory named test at any depth, with rg -g '!test/**', an anchored glob that at most excludes a top-level test directory. File sets and match counts were never compared.

The .gitignore parser matches patterns against the bare name or the path relative to the search root, not relative to the .gitignore's own directory, so leading-slash rules ('/build') never match, path rules in nested .gitignore files misfire, lines longer than 255 bytes are split into separate rules, and rules past 512 are dropped silently.

Several README claims do not match the code: the literal kernel probes 16 bytes per step, not 64; the printer is one shared buffer, not thread-local; the reader still calls fstat on every file; and the 'up to 40x' tagline is not supported by any published row (maximum 8.4x).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Like oxsv (SIMD C CLI that claims a large lead over a Rust tool, xsv), chingrep is best treated as readable sample code rather than a replacement; pick it over asmlib's strstr/memmem when you specifically want an AArch64 NEON assembly first/last-byte filter, and pick ripgrep itself for real searches.
verified_claims_summary: arena/run-arena.sh timed chingrep 1.0.0 (clang -O3, ARM64 NEON build) against ripgrep 15.2.0 on an unnamed Apple Silicon Mac over the author's private 17,000-file 'treesource' folder, best of 3 runs each via Python perf_counter around subprocess.run, with a warm-up only for chingrep: 1,870.9 ms vs 12,470.7 ms summed over 22 scenarios (6.7x), around 87 ms vs 640 ms for unfiltered literal searches, 27.9 vs 37.9 ms with a *.c filter and a loss on stdin (3.6 vs 3.5 ms). Because the two tools almost certainly searched different file sets (ripgrep's unfiltered time stays near 640 ms regardless of hit count while its *.c run takes 38 ms), the ratio mostly measures what each tool chooses to skip, not search speed.
status_note: Brand-new single-author repo (8 commits between 2026-10-05 and 2026-10-08, 0 stars, no issues, no releases), MIT-licensed and small enough to read in an hour, but macOS-only in practice and with a line-numbering bug, so treat it as reference code rather than a ripgrep replacement.
